 1                                        I.   INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.   My name is Jonah B. Mauldin. My business address is the New Mexico Public Regulation

 4        Commission (“Commission”, “NMPRC”, or “PRC”), 1596 Pacheco St., Santa Fe, NM

 5        87505.

 6   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR POSITION WITH THE COMMISSION?

 7   A.   I am the Accounting Bureau Chief with the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission –

 8        Utility Division (“Staff”).

 9   Q.   DID YOU PREVIOUSLY FILE DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

10   A.   Yes, my prepared direct testimony was filed in this case on May 1, 2026.

11   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS TESTIMONY?

12   A.   My testimony provides discussion regarding why Staff was not a signatory to the

13        Stipulation filed on June 22, 2026. This testimony will also address certain provisions of

14        the settlement term sheet filed in this case.

15   Q.   WHO ARE THE WITNESSES PROVIDING TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION OF

16        STIPULATION ON BEHALF OF STAFF IN THIS CASE?

17   A.   The witnesses providing testimony in opposition in this case, on behalf of Staff, are Dr.

18        Larry Blank, Daren K. Zigich, Ed Rilkoff, and Peterson Brossy.


19                                 II.         BACKGROUND

20   Q.   CAN YOU PROVIDE A BRIEF OVERVIEW OF SPS’S APPLICATION?


                                                     1
                                               NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                    TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                                      JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.         Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS” or the “Company”) filed an application with

 2              the Commission requesting approval to increase its base rates and to obtain various

 3              additional approvals related to its cost of service, capital investments, and ratemaking

 4              treatment. SPS’s Initial Application sought a base rate revenue increase for the New

 5              Mexico retail jurisdiction of $175,354,544, or about a 24.45 percent increase in base rate

 6              revenues.1 Subsequently, on March 20, 2026, SPS filed a Comprehensive List of Revisions

 7              which reflected a net decrease to SPS’s Future Test Year revenue deficiency of $3,054,395.

 8              Shortly after, on March 25, 2026, SPS submitted notice of a correction to its Future Test

 9              Year depreciation expense, which reduces total company depreciation expense by

10              $11,833,0812 and reduces SPS’s New Mexico Retail Future Test Year revenue requirement

11              by $4,748,791. Thus, SPS’s revised requested base rate revenue increase was

12              approximately $167,551,358.

13   Q.         WHAT WAS STAFF’S REVENUE DEFICIENCY AS SUPPORTED IN DIRECT

14              TESTIMONY?

15   A.         Staff’s revenue deficiency, as presented in direct testimony, is $ 47,691,101, or about a

16              6.65% increase in base rate revenues.

17   Q.         HOW        DID     STAFF        DERRIVE          THEIR   RECOMMENDED         REVENUE

18              DEFICINCY?

19   A.         Staff’s revenue deficiency is a result of adjustments that were supported throughout the

20              direct testimony of Staff witnesses.


     1
         Direct Testimony of Zoë E. Lees, 18:18-22.
     2
         $4,955,448 New Mexico Retail.

 1   Q.         WHAT IS THE REVENUE DEFICIENCY AGREED TO BY SIGNATORIES TO

 2              THE STIPULATION?

 3   A.         The stipulation in this case would authorize SPS to implement an increase in New Mexico

 4              retail base rate revenues of $90,000,000, or approximately 12.55%, effective December 1,

 5              2026.3


 6                           III.         SUMMARY OF THIS TESTIMONY

 7   Q.         PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR OVERALL POSITION REGARDING THE

 8              STIPULATION.

 9   A.         While the Stipulation reflects movement from SPS's original proposal in certain respects,

10              it does not adequately address the concerns Staff raised in its Direct Testimony. The

11              stipulated revenue increase of $90 million is nearly double Staff's recommended deficiency

12              of $47,691,101, and as illustrated in Table JBM-1, a significant portion of that gap is not

13              explained by the Stipulation and is not transparent. Staff's positions on the specific terms

14              addressed in this testimony are summarized below.

15              The withdrawal of the property tax and excess liability insurance (“ELI”) expense trackers

16              is consistent with Staff's Direct Testimony and Staff supports those provisions. While the

17              Stipulation's treatment of the ELI regulatory asset moves in the right direction by extending

18              amortization beyond SPS's proposed two years, in my opinion, as stated in my Direct

19              Testimony, it does not go far enough. In addition, the Stipulation is silent on the regulatory



     3
         Contested Stipulation filed June 22, 2026.
                                                             3
                                      NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                           TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                          JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1        asset balance and the three-year amortization period results in annual expense that is

 2        materially higher than Staff's recommendation of a four-year amortization period.

 3        Likewise, the Stipulation's removal of the request for recovery of Southwest Power Pool

 4        (“SPP”) deficiency payments and removal of the FPPCAC request from this proceeding,

 5        while consistent with my Direct Testimony, still does not go far enough to prevent future

 6        recovery of these costs, instead creating a broader deferral mechanism that encompasses

 7        costs that go beyond what SPS originally requested. Staff views this provision as a net

 8        negative for ratepayers.


 9                       IV.         REVENUE REQUIREMENT

10   Q.   WHAT IS THE REVENUE                   REQUIREMENT           AGREED        TO BY THE

11        SIGNATORIES AND HOW DOES IT COMPARE TO SPS'S REQUEST AND

12        STAFF'S RECOMMENDATION?

13   A.   The Stipulation authorizes SPS to implement a base rate revenue increase of $90,000,000.

14        Table JBM-1 below presents a comparison of SPS's proposed, stipulated, and Staff's

15        recommended revenue deficiencies, including itemized reductions for each. As shown in

16        Panel A, SPS's original proposed deficiency of $175,354,544 was reduced to a revised

17        deficiency of $167,551,358 following post-filing corrections. Panel B presents the

18        stipulated deficiency of $90,000,000, which reflects approximately $77.6 million in

19        reductions from SPS's revised deficiency amount. Of that amount, approximately $41.6

20        million is attributable to identified Stipulation terms, while $35.9 million represents non-

21        defined reductions that are not explained by the Stipulation's express terms and are “black

 2   Q.   WHY DOES STAFF OPPOSE THE STIPULATED REVENUE REQUIREMENT?

 3   A.   First, Staff opposes the stipulated revenue requirement because it does not reflect the

 4        adjustments Staff determined to be necessary to produce fair, just, and reasonable rates. In

 5        addition, the $42.3 million gap between Staff's recommended revenue deficiency and the

 6        stipulated amount is not adequately explained by the stipulation's terms, as illustrated by

 7        the non-defined, not transparent, reductions in Panel B of Table JBM-1. The Stipulation

 8        also does not address specific concerns Staff raised in direct testimony--most notably the

 9        concerns raised by Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank in his Direct Testimony and his testimony

10        in opposition to the Stipulation regarding jurisdictional allocation. Moreover, while the

11        Stipulation’s $90 million increase in base revenue is about half of SPS’s original request,

12        it is still nearly double Staff's recommended increase of $47 million and still presents



                                                                   6
                                         NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                            TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                            JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1        significant affordability concerns, which are addressed in the Direct Testimony and

 2        Testimony in Opposition to the Stipulation of Staff witness Ed Rilkoff.

 3   Q.   ARE THERE ADDITIONAL CONCERNS WITH THE STIPULATED REVENUE

 4        REQUIREMENT?

 5   A.   Yes. The stipulated revenue increase of $90 million raises significant affordability

 6        concerns, particularly for residential and small commercial customers who have limited

 7        ability to absorb large rate increases.

 8   Q.   DOES YOUR TESTIMONY ADDRESS SPECIFIC COMPONENTS OF THE

 9        STIPULATION THAT RELATE TO YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

10   A.   Yes. The Stipulation's treatment of SPP deficiency payments, the ELI regulatory asset

11        amortization, and the withdrawal of the property tax and ELI expense trackers each relate

12        to positions taken in my direct testimony. Those terms are addressed in the subsequent

13        sections of this testimony.

14   Q.   DOES STAFF WITNESS PETERSON BROSSY ALSO ADDRESS STIPULATION

15        TERMS RELATED TO HIS DIRECT TESTIMONY?

16   A.   Yes. Staff witness Peterson Brossy’s Testimony in Opposition to Stipulation addresses

17        stipulation terms that relate to positions taken in his Direct Testimony.


18                    V.         SHORT TERM CAPACITY NEEDS

19   Q.   WHAT DID SPS ORIGINALLY REQUEST REGARDING SPP DEFICIENCY

20        PAYMENTS?



                                                    7
                                                NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                    TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                                      JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.         SPS requested authority to recover a projected SPP deficiency payment of approximately

 2              $4,931,594, on a New Mexico retail basis, through the FPPCAC, with a tracker mechanism

 3              as an alternative.4

 4   Q.         WHAT DOES THE STIPULATION DO WITH THAT REQUEST?

 5   A.         Section 1.5 of the Stipulation withdraws SPS's request to recover SPP deficiency payments

 6              through the FPPCAC without prejudice. It requires SPS to use its best efforts to address

 7              short-term capacity needs through capacity purchases in lieu of deficiency payments,

 8              “where prudent.”5 Any capacity purchases or deficiency payments incurred through the

 9              effective date of new rates from SPS's next base rate case will be deferred as a regulatory

10              asset, subject to an annual New Mexico cap of $10 million, with recovery to be sought in

11              a future proceeding, with all parties reserving the right to contest the reasonableness and

12              recoverability of any such deferrals.

13   Q.         WHAT WAS STAFF'S POSITION IN DIRECT TESTIMONY?

14   A.         In my Direct Testimony, I recommended denial of SPP deficiency payment recovery-- in

15              its entirety. Staff's position was that these payments are compliance penalties resulting

16              from a failure of SPS to meet its SPP capacity obligations, which are not fuel or purchased

17              power costs eligible for FPPCAC recovery; And that SPS had not demonstrated the

18              projected deficiency was not the result of its own imprudent planning. Accordingly, Staff

19              opposed recovery through the FPPCAC, a tracker, or any other mechanism.

20   Q.         DOES STAFF SUPPORT THE STIPULATION'S TREATMENT OF THIS ISSUE?


     4
         Direct Testimony of Zoë E. Lees, pp.41-44.
     5
         Stipulation, Section1.5.
                                                             8
                                                 NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                     TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                                    JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.         It is Staff's Direct position that compliance penalties should not be recoverable from

 2              customers and therefore SPS’s request for deficiency payment recovery from its customers

 3              should be denied, not merely deferred to some future proceeding. That said, should the

 4              Commission decide to adopt the Stipulation, deferral of the issue would be preferable to

 5              approving recovery of the deficiency payments now, and the $10 million annual cap on

 6              costs would provide some protection for ratepayers in the interim. Therefore, Staff does

 7              not formally oppose this provision of the Stipulation.

 8   Q.         DOES THE STIPULATION'S REQUIREMENT THAT SPS USE BEST EFFORTS

 9              TO       PURSUE              SHORT-TERM         CAPACITY     PURCHASES        PROVIDE

10              MEANINGFUL PROTECTION FOR RATEPAYERS?

11   A.         No. SPS's own Direct testimony acknowledged that it was already evaluating short-term

12              capacity purchases as an alternative to deficiency payments, and simultaneously

13              represented that it could not procure short-term resources to resolve the capacity deficit

14              because developers withdrew from negotiations following SPS's 2024 All-Source RFP.6

15              Therefore, the best efforts requirement is not a meaningful improvement over what has

16              already represented it was doing.

17   Q.         DOES THE STIPULATION REPRESENT A NET IMPROVEMENT OVER SPS'S

18              ORIGINAL REQUEST REGARDING THE DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS?

19   A.         SPS's original request was limited to recovery of SPP deficiency payments through the

20              FPPCAC, with a tracker as an alternative. The Stipulation removes the FPPCAC request



     6
         Id. pp. 42-43, lines 15-17 & 1-4.
                                                            9
                                                NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT

 1              but creates a broader deferral mechanism that encompasses both deficiency payments and

 2              short-term capacity purchases. Short-term capacity purchases were not part of SPS's

 3              original alternative tracker request and would not have been recoverable until incorporated

 4              into rates. The Stipulation therefore expands the scope of costs that SPS may seek to

 5              recover in a future proceeding beyond what SPS originally requested in this case. Staff

 6              views this aspect of the Stipulation as a net negative for ratepayers and is the primary basis

 7              for not fully supporting Section 1.5 of the Stipulation pertaining to short term capacity and

 8              SPP deficiency payments.


 9                  VI.      RECOVERY MECHANISMS FOR VARIABLE COSTS

10   Q.         WHAT DID SPS ORIGINALLY REQUEST REGARDING VARIABLE COST

11              RECOVERY MECHANISMS?

12   A.         SPS requested authorization to establish two prospective tracking and deferral

13              mechanisms. First, SPS requested a property tax tracker that would record the annual

14              difference between property tax expense included in rates and actual property taxes

15              incurred, with any resulting balance deferred for recovery or refund in its next rate case.

16              Second, SPS requested an ELI expense tracker that would record the annual difference

17              between the ELI premium level included in base rates and actual ELI premiums incurred,

18              similarly deferred for future recovery or refund.7

19   Q.         WHAT DOES THE STIPULATION DO WITH THESE REQUESTS?



     7
         Direct Testimony of Zoë E. Lees, pp. 94-98.
                                                              10
                                        NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                             TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                           JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.     Section 1.6 of the Stipulation withdraws both requests.

 2   Q.     DOES STAFF SUPPORT THIS PROVISION OF THE STIPULATION?

 3   A.     Yes. Withdrawal of SPS’s requests for both trackers is consistent with Staff's Direct

 4          testimony, which recommended denial of both mechanisms. Staff supports this provision

 5          for the reasons outlined in my direct testimony.


 6   VII.       RECOVERY OF REGULATORY ASSETS AND DEFERRALS

 7                                       A. ELI Regulatory Asset

 8   Q.     WHAT      DID     SPS    ORIGINALLY          PROPOSE       REGARDING         THE     ELI

 9          REGULATORY ASSET?

10   A.     SPS proposed recovery of the deferred ELI regulatory asset with a balance of

11          approximately $28 million on a New Mexico retail basis, amortized over two years,

12          resulting in annual amortization expense of approximately $14.1 million.

13   Q.     WHAT DOES THE STIPULATION PROVIDE REGARDING THE ELI

14          REGULATORY ASSET?

15   A.     The Stipulation authorizes recovery of the deferred ELI regulatory asset over a three-year

16          amortization period, resulting in annual amortization expense of approximately $9.4

17          million. The Stipulation does not address the regulatory asset balance, therefore Staff is

18          under the assumption the balance will be set at SPS’s requested amount.

19   Q.     WHAT WAS STAFF'S POSITION IN DIRECT TESTIMONY?




                                                    11
                                      NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                            TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO STIPULATION OF
                                          JONAH B. MAULDIN
 1   A.   In my Direct testimony, I recommended reducing the regulatory asset balance to

 2        approximately $26 million based on updated roll forward data provided by SPS in

 3        discovery, and amortizing that balance over four years, resulting in annual amortization

 4        expense of approximately $6.6 million. Staff's recommended adjustments result in a

 5        reduction to the revenue requirement of approximately $7.6 million compared to SPS's

 6        original proposal.

 7   Q.   WHY DOES STAFF NOT SUPPORT THIS PROVISION OF THE STIPULATION?

 8   A.   Staff does not formally oppose this provision but has two primary concerns that prevent it

 9        supporting it: First, the Stipulation is silent on the regulatory asset balance, leaving SPS's

10        proposed balance of approximately $28 million unaddressed. As discussed in Staff's Direct

11        testimony, SPS's own updated discovery responses support a lower balance of

12        approximately $26 million. Accepting SPS's higher balance without adjustment results in

13        approximately $2 million in overstated costs being embedded in rates. Second, the

14        Stipulation's three-year amortization period results in annual amortization expense of

15        approximately $9.4 million, is $2.8 million per year higher than Staff's recommended $6.6

16        million. While the Stipulation represents movement in the right direction (increasing

17        amortization to three years from SPS's proposed two-year amortization), it does not go far

18        enough to adequately protect ratepayers from the rate impact of this regulatory asset

19        recovery.

                                          JONAH B. MAULDIN

 1                             B. Legacy Meters and Community Solar

 2   Q.   DOES YOUR TESTIMONY ADDRESS THE STIPULATION'S TREATMENT OF

 3        LEGACY METER AMORTIZATION AND COMMUNITY SOLAR PROGRAM

 4        COSTS?

 5   A.   No. Those provisions relate to positions taken in Staff witness Peterson Brossy's direct

 6        testimony. Mr. Brossy addresses those terms in his testimony in opposition.


 7                              VIII.         CONCLUSION

 8   Q.   DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCLUDING REMARKS?

 9   A.   Yes. The positions Staff presented in its Direct testimony were carefully developed and

10        supported by substantial evidence in the record. While Staff acknowledges that the

11        Stipulation represents compromise and movement on certain issues, it does not resolve the

12        fundamental concerns Staff identified regarding SPS's proposed revenue requirement and

13        specific cost recovery requests and jurisdictional allocation. Staff does not believe the

14        Stipulation as a whole adequately protects ratepayers and maintains the positions presented

15        in its Direct testimony as the more appropriate basis for the Commission's determination

16        in this proceeding. Other Staff witnesses addressing the Stipulation in their respective

17        testimonies in opposition will speak to the terms within their areas of expertise.

18   Q.   DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR TESTIMONY?

19   A.   Yes.
